questions.:question/problem:
Find where the normal line to the curve $y=4\sqrt{x}+x-1$ at the point with $x$-coordinate $1$ intersects the $x$-axis.

The intersection is $(${{field-1}}$,$ {{field-2}}$)$. Give exact values.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
First find the point on the curve.

$$
f(1)=4\sqrt{(1)}+(1)-1=4.
$$

The normal passes through $(1,4)$.

Rewrite the radical or reciprocal using powers, then differentiate.

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x)&=4 x^{\frac{1}{2}} + x - 1, \\f'(x)&=1 + \frac{2}{x^{\frac{1}{2}}}=1 + \frac{2}{\sqrt{x}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the tangent slope and take its negative reciprocal to find the normal slope.

$$
\begin{aligned}
m_t=f'(1)&=1 + \frac{2}{\sqrt{(1)}}=3, \\m_n=-\frac{1}{m_t}&=-\frac{1}{(3)}=- \frac{1}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Use point-slope form through $(1,4)$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
y-(4)&=- \frac{1}{3}(x-(1)), \\y&=- \frac{x}{3} + \frac{13}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

At the $x$-axis, $y=0$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
0&=- \frac{1}{3}x+\left(\frac{13}{3}\right), \\x&=13.
\end{aligned}
$$

The intersection is $(13,0)$.

Find where the normal line to the curve $y=4-{x}^{2}$ at the point $(1,3)$ intersects the $x$-axis.

The normal line intersects the $x$-axis at
$($
{{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}} $).$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4-{x}^{2})=-2x.
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(1)=-2(1)=-2,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(-2)}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-3 & =\frac{1}{2}(x-1) \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{2}+3 \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{5}{2} & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}x & =-\frac{5}{2} \\ x & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(\,-5,0\,).$

The normal line intersects the $x$-axis at

questions.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
f'(x)=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(18 x^{2} - 36 x + 30)=36 x - 36.
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m=f'(0)=-36=-36,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
m'=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(-36)}=\frac{1}{36}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(30)&=\frac{1}{36}(x-(0))\\y&=\frac{1}{36}x+30.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{36}x+30&=0\\\frac{1}{36}x&=-30\\x&=-1080.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(-1080,0).$

$$

$$

Evaluate the tangent slope and take its negative reciprocal to find the normal slope.

$$
\begin{aligned}

At the $y$-axis, $x=0$.

$$

y&=\frac{1}{4}\cdot 0+(-21), \\y&=-21.

Find where the normal line to the curve $y=\frac{20}{x}+10$ at the point $(1,30)$ intersects the $x$-axis.

The normal line intersects the $x$-axis at

questions.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(\frac{20}{x}+10\right)\\&=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(10 + \frac{20}{x}\right)\\&=-20x^{-2}\\&=- \frac{20}{x^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m=f'(1)=-20=-20,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
m'=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(-20)}=\frac{1}{20}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(30)&=\frac{1}{20}(x-(1))\\y&=\frac{1}{20}x-\left(\frac{1}{20}\right)+(30)\\y&=\frac{1}{20}x+\frac{599}{20}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{20}x+\frac{599}{20}&=0\\x&=-599.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the  $x$-axis at $(-599,0).$

questions.:question/problem:
Find where the normal line to the curve $y=3\sqrt{x}$ at the point $(4,6)$ intersects the $y$-axis.

The normal line intersects the $y$-axis at $(${{field-1}}$,$ {{field-2}}$)$. Give exact values.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Rewrite the radical as a fractional power and differentiate:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x)&=3x^{1/2},\\
f'(x)&=\frac{3}{2}x^{-1/2}=\frac{3}{2\sqrt{x}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

At $(4,6)$, the tangent slope and normal slope are

$$
f'(4)=\frac{3}{2\sqrt{4}}=\frac{3}{4},\qquad m_n=-\frac{1}{3/4}=-\frac{4}{3}.
$$

The normal passes through $(4,6)$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
y-6&=-\frac{4}{3}(x-4),\\
y&=-\frac{4}{3}x+\frac{16}{3}+6\\
&=-\frac{4}{3}x+\frac{34}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

At the $y$-axis, $x=0$, giving $y=\frac{34}{3}$. The intersection is $\left(0,\frac{34}{3}\right)$.

questions.:question/problem:
Let $f(x)=2\sqrt{x}-3x+1$. Find where the normal line to the curve $y=f(x)$ at the point with $x$-coordinate $4$ intersects the $x$-axis.

The normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(${{field-1}}$,$ {{field-2}}$)$. Give exact values.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
First find the point on the curve:

$$
f(4)=2\sqrt{4}-3(4)+1=4-12+1=-7.
$$

Thus the normal passes through $(4,-7)$. Differentiate both variable terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x)&=2x^{1/2}-3x+1,\\
f'(x)&=x^{-1/2}-3=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}-3.
\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent slope is

$$
f'(4)=\frac{1}{2}-3=-\frac{5}{2}.
$$

The normal slope is the negative reciprocal, so

$$
m_n=-\frac{1}{-5/2}=\frac{2}{5}.
$$

Using $(4,-7)$, the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}
y+7&=\frac{2}{5}(x-4),\\
y&=\frac{2}{5}x-\frac{8}{5}-7\\
&=\frac{2}{5}x-\frac{43}{5}.
\end{aligned}
$$

At the $x$-axis, $y=0$. Solving gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
0&=\frac{2}{5}x-\frac{43}{5},\\
2x&=43,\\
x&=\frac{43}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The intersection is $\left(\frac{43}{2},0\right)$.

questions.:question/problem:
Find where the normal line to the curve $y={x}^{3}$ at the point $(1,1)$ intersects the $x$-axis.

The normal line intersects the $x$-axis at

{{field-1}}$,$

questions.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3})=3{x}^{2}.
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(1)=3(1)^{2}=3,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =-\frac{1}{3}(x-(1)) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{1}{3}+1 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{4}{3} & =0 \\ \frac{1}{3}x & =\frac{4}{3} \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(\,4,0\,).$
